Whenever I recall the turmoil of my ancestral kingdom,
I inscribe these verses in the year of Gengzi;
I have become a man of the Righteous Emperor.
Holding the Classic of Mountains and Seas in hand,
with a wine-straining cloth upon his head,
his spirit pursues the solitary clouds into the distance.
Regarding the "Discourse on the Bird Returning to Its Nest," I have not yet seen the complete text.
As for the "Jianji Guan" (Observation of Simplicity and Stillness) by Zhang Yu: Under the Zixiao Peak, the hermit’s thatched hall remains;
For a thousand years, only the stone chime is left hanging empty.
White vapors arise at night as dragons dwell in the water;
azure clouds sever in autumn as cranes return to heaven.
The shadow of the bamboo chamber occupies the moonlight in the central courtyard.
The sound from the pine railing comes from the spring halfway up the cliff;
tomorrow again there will be the sorrows of this floating world.
The dreams remain as they were, piling up in vain across the entire mountain.

Observing the Provinces on a Spring Day: Resting for the First Time at Dongxi Lin Monastery. By Wei Yingwu. Taking advantage of the season to inspect local customs, I have come to rest for the first time at Dongxi Lin Monastery.
Bestowing kindness upon the elderly,
he set forth from Xunyang with his falcon-bannered carriage,
arranging his team to roam the mountains and rivers.
The white snow gathers as the ravines clear;
a multitude of peaks stand arrayed against the distant sky.
The craggy stone gate bears a formidable shape.
The incense burner smoke drifts in the deep mists;
amidst the overgrown brush, I have repeatedly been caught in snares.
Leaning precariously, I am on the verge of falling headlong.
Now I have finally reached the monastery of the Śākya clan;
the seasonal objects there are repeatedly beautiful and elegant.
In the past, Tanyuan first initiated its construction.
In this secluded and profound place,
the bamboo grove temples to the east and west are fed by the flowing waters of cold mountain streams.
Human affairs have long since vanished;
the years and months have further stretched on.
Only the temple halls remain, their colors still crimson and azure.
The stone steps and pavilions all lean precariously;
former practitioners have also dwelt here.
With a virtuous body, he has severed all worldly ties.
Now I have received the sovereign's trust;
I spread the teachings throughout the villages and neighborhoods.
If only I can grasp the subtle mystery of the Way, [all will be well].
In managing affairs, he was impartial;
his mind always shared in what was esteemed.
How could his traces have avoided being entangled?
Inscribed on the Study of My Cousin Xu at Xilin Hermitage Sharing this space with my cousin, we have both begun to settle our minds in the twilight years;
yet you, who have stilled your heart, remain youthful in spirit.
Longing for the Xie Shijing Monastery,
Wen followed the monks to behold its wonders;
a clear spring poured down upon the front steps.
The clear pond reflects light upon the northern window;
fruits and medicinal herbs spread their various fragrances;
pines and bamboos stand sparse yet steep with age.
I have frequently ascended to the realms of recluses and often indulged in gazing from these fragrant heights;
I have even explored the chestnut-nut caves of the black monkeys.
Gathering mushrooms by the forests and ridges,
how can linen robes ward off the cold?
Eating simple vegetables, they are no remedy for hunger.
Though you may dwell alone in a humble lane to the north,
how could you remain cold when the purple and violet robes shine?
Your commandery possesses the "couch for honoring the worthy."
In the morning, the assembled scholars flatter you,
wishing to share your carriage with its crimson wheels;
do not fear the reproach of official correspondence.
Inscription on the "Hermitage of Bequeathed Kindness" at the Residence of Attendant Censor Zheng, Composed Together with the Layman Jin Yi Seng.
Amidst the green mountains, he has built a thatched cottage.
Sparse pines reflect the evening mist;
the spring pond holds mossy green.
Lush vegetation overtops the sunny ridges.
The cries of new birds echo through the secluded valley;
with a long whistle, I climb the lofty trees.
I admire these high footsteps of those who transcend the world.
Composed at the Base of the Waterfall in the Western Gorge of Jianji Hermitage (same as the preceding): The cascading stream scatters over the sheer cliff;
Numinous mist rises deep within the emerald ravine.
Pine winds arise at the edge of the cliffs;
drifting and fluttering, they wash the dust from my breast.
Peering through the lattice, I observe the monkeys and crows.
Unfastening my official robes, I disperse among the forested clouds;
with tea and fruit, I invite my true companions.
With wine and cups, we satisfy our shared hearts.
For many years I have cherished this appreciation;
now that spring has arrived, I come to seek it once more.
I shall simply take up my transverse flute.
First, recording the sounds of mountains and waters:
Seeking the Waterfall at Jianji Hermitage. As before, I tread upon precarious stones to cross the rushing ravine;
I climb the distant cliffs to play with the suspended spring.
I shall continue to count the years by the tiger-skin and bamboo slips;
I wish to entrust my return to the world, severing all worldly ties.
Jianji Hermitage, Jianji Hermitage: The numinous traces beyond the mundane are rarely visited by guests. —By Qin Taoyu.
Bamboo huts lean against the old wisteria gate;
ten thousand scrolls of vermilion-scripted books lie within.
A thousand layers of azure peaks lock away the misty green heights.
The white monkey weeping in the dew departs with its young;
the dark crane crying in the wind returns to the person’s side.
Only the name upon the Jade Gate shall endure forever.
At twilight, idle clouds drift through the void on their own.
Waterfall, waterfall! Lu Chan’s true source is unfathomable to men;
a thousand feet it hangs from the edge of the clouds.
The colors of the mountain peaks cannot be stained;
divine craftsmanship makes them difficult to fashion.
In summer, they spray mist where monkeys and birds stand still.
In autumn, the spray splashes upon the Dipper and Ox;
after waiting for salvation at the vast blue ocean,
the surging waves are even more beautiful to behold.
The Translation Platform: The Translation Platform is surrounded by wild vines from Yoshino and stands high above the valley floor;
the records of previous dynasties are not in error.
Here, golden script translates ancient verses.
Chinese characters have transformed into Hu script;
colored threads have snapped, blown away by the wind;
yellowed silk remains as the residue of a fire’s ashes.
It pierces the clouds to reveal the white sun;
it penetrates the water to illuminate the lotuses.
The tadpoles undergo frequent transformations.
How many times has the hermitage garden been weeded?
Your true gate and refined style both cause me to long for the likes of Sima Xiangru.
Inscription on the Old Hall of the Late Director Xiao at Xilin Monastery By Han Yu: The Director had a daughter who was able to transmit his legacy.
Baidao had no son to protect his lineage;
having happened upon the place where he once dwelt on Kuangshan,
a few lines of sorrowful tears fall amidst the mist and clouds.
Waterfall, waterfall! Xu Ning’s cascading spring, cascading spring—its flow is as straight as a bamboo pole.
Like thunder rushing to the sea without a moment's rest, it has flown like a white silk ribbon through all time, from antiquity to the present.

"A single stream cuts through the color of the green mountains. *Visiting the Old Residence of Lord Tao, with Preface* By Bai Juyi I have long admired the character of Tao Yuanming. I have heard that when he was alive, he lived in seclusion at Lingshi, and that his old residence still exists today. Therefore, I have traveled from afar to visit it. Upon arriving, I found only a few dilapidated dwellings; the surrounding fields were overgrown with weeds, and the traces of the past were difficult to discern. I gazed upon the ruins and sighed deeply. I composed this poem to record my feelings. The old residence of the former lord remains, Yet the weeds grow thick and the traces are lost. A single stream cuts through the color of the green mountains, And the setting sun casts its shadow upon the ancient trees. The wild geese fly back toward their homes, While the spring wind blows across the empty courtyard. I stand alone, gazing at the ruins, My heart filled with sorrow for the man of old. How could I not feel a deep longing? For the sake of the man who lived here, I have come from afar to visit these remains. I gaze at the ruins and sigh deeply; My tears fall as I recall his life. He was truly one who knew how to live; His spirit surely dwells among the clouds. I wish to follow in his footsteps, But alas, I am already too old. I shall return to my own home, And there I shall cultivate my own lotus. May I never again be stained by the world, But always remain pure and unblemished. (From *Complete Tang Poetry*, Vol. 30)
In years past, while living in leisure by the Wei River,
I composed sixteen poems in the style of Tao Qian.
Now, I am traveling through Mount Lu.
Passing through the old home of Chaisang,
I thought of that man and sought out his residence;
I could not remain silent.
Furthermore, he inscribed a poem which says:
"Dust and grime do not defile jade;
the numinous phoenix does not peck at mutton fat."
Alas, Tao Jingjie! Born during the interval between the Jin and Song dynasties,
his heart truly possessed that which he upheld.
In the end, his mouth could not utter a word.
I contemplate forever the bamboo-clad man of solitude;
he shook out his robes on Mount Shouyang.
Bo Yi and Shu Qi were each but single individuals;
that they suffered from hunger and destitution was not difficult for them.
But you, Master, have five sons.
They shared his hunger and cold;
the food in their bellies was insufficient,
and the clothing on their bodies was incomplete.
Even when summoned repeatedly, he did not rise;
he may truly be called a man of genuine worth.
I was born after your reign.
Five hundred years have passed since he lived;
whenever I read the biography of Wuliu,
my eyes envision him and my heart remains deeply devoted.
In the past, I once composed sixteen chapters in verse to celebrate his enduring legacy;
now I have come to visit his former residence.
When Senjia was before the ruler,
he did not long for the wine in the goblet,
nor did he long for the zither without strings.
Longing for you, I renounce honor and profit;
I shall grow old and die here in this secluded villa.
Chaisang is an ancient village.
In the old mountains of Lili, the rivers and peaks remain;
the chrysanthemums beneath the fence are no longer seen,
yet only the smoke from the ruins lingers on.
Although his descendants have heard [of this],
their clan name has not yet changed;
whenever they encounter someone surnamed Tao, [they feel a sense of kinship].
It causes my heart to remain as it was.
A Spring Excursion to Erlinsi. On a spring excursion to Erlinsi, following the previous [poem], I dismounted at Xilin Temple.
With a carefree air, I advanced on light crutches.
In the morning I am an official in the government office;
by evening, I am a guest on Mount Ling.
In the second month, Mount Kuanglu is still frozen.
The snow has begun to melt away;
on the sunlit thickets, tea buds emerge,
while from the shaded crevices, the veins of the spring seep forth.
Joyful and flourishing, the climate is warm;
dense and lush, the clouds and mists accumulate.
They disperse to form ten thousand blossoms in springtime.
Concentrated into a single breath of azure clarity;
with the body at ease, one easily attains serenity.
When official duties are dispersed, there is no longer any compulsion.
Those eighteen worthies were the same in their conduct throughout antiquity and the present;
in this year, following the custom of the capping ceremony, military conflict arose everywhere.
The wise man exerts his mind in planning;
the military officers are engaged in campaigns and levies.
Yet there remains one who is devoid of talent.
Amidst the mountains, I toyed with the springs and rocks;
I wandered through the Shimen Gorge. As before, there was no old path at Shimen;
I cleared away the brambles to seek out the traces of the past.
At this time, I encounter autumn by the mountains and waters;
its pure radiance is as it was in ages past.
I have often heard of those such as Huiyuan.
I have inscribed this poem upon the cliff face;
clouds cover it, sealed by moss.
It is a somber gray, beyond all seeking.
Sparse wild bamboo; crumbled and weathered stones from many years ago.
Since the time of the Eastern Jin dynasty, [this place has remained thus].
No more do people travel here;
there is only the sound of the autumn stream.
Its murmuring flows empty through morning and evening.

Inscription on Yuan’s Eighteen-River Pavilion at the Foot of Mount Wulao, Southeast of Mount Lu I share with you the same sentiment as before: I find it strange that you do not take pleasure in official service.
Furthermore, he did not travel through the towns and villages;
today he has arrived at this secluded dwelling.
Now I clearly understand the reason why.
I stayed overnight at your Stone Brook Pavilion;
the sound of the murmuring stream filled my ears.
I drank your wine from a conch-shell cup.
Lying drunk, unable to rise,
I gaze upon your Five Elders Peak;
my regret for dwelling in the city grows ever deeper.
I love your three sons; at first, I lamented that I had no children of my own.
I am currently beneath the peak of Lufeng.
He built a hut to become a lay practitioner;
from this point on, the coming and going between the north side of the mountain and the south side began.
Composed upon the occasion of newly establishing a thatched cottage below Mount Xianglu;
these verses on my reflections are inscribed upon a rock facing the northern side of Mount Xianglu.
To the west of Yiai Temple,
how carved is the white stone;
the clear stream flows with a murmuring sound.
There are several dozen pine trees and more than a thousand bamboo stalks;
the pines spread out emerald parasols.
Bamboo leans against the azure *langgan* trees;
beneath them, no one dwells.
Alas, how many years have passed!
At times, monkeys and birds gather;
all day long, the wind and smoke are empty.
Occasionally, there is a son of deep obscurity.
My surname is Bái and my given name is Lètiān.
Throughout my life I have had no particular attachments;
yet upon seeing this, my heart remains as it was before.
As if having attained a place for the end of life,
suddenly one does not know how to return;
building upon the cliffs, one constructs a thatched hut.
I cleave the ravines to open tea gardens;
with what shall I cleanse my ears?
A flying spring falls from above the eaves.
"How shall my eyes be purified?
Beneath the steps, white lotuses grow.
In his left hand he carries a platform; in his right, he holds a five-stringed lute."
Proud and self-sufficient in spirit,
he sat with legs spread wide among them;
intoxicated by his inspiration, he looked up to heaven and sang.
I have briefly entrusted these words to this song.
I am originally a man of the wilds,
yet I was mistakenly dragged into the net of the world.
In youth I once came to attend the rising sun;
now aged, I return to the mountains.
Like a weary bird finding a lush tree, I have found my refuge.
A dried-up fish returns to the clear source;
abandoning this, where would one go?
The human world is full of perils and hardships.
Ascending the Summit of Mount Xianglu: Ascending the summit of Mount Xianglu is as described before—far, far away is Mount Xianglu.
If one keeps it in mind with the ears and eyes, yet spends one’s whole life being harnessed by external things, [one will never reach it].
Only today have I set out;
climbing the creepers and treading upon precarious rocks,
my hands and feet weary from constant bending and stretching.
There were three or four people traveling together;
two did not dare to ascend.
Upon reaching the summit of the peak, [he remained there].
The eyes spin and the spirit grows dazed;
its height and depth reach ten thousand fathoms,
and its breadth and narrowness intersect beyond counting.
Without exhausting the realms of sight and hearing,
how can one know the vastness of the universe?
The waters of the Yangtze River appear as thin as a cord.
The city of Pen is smaller than the palm of my hand;
why do I weary myself in vain?
I have not yet been able to cast off the fetters of the mundane world.
Returning home, my thoughts are naturally unsettled;
bowing my head, I enter the ant-hills.
Staying overnight at Jianji Hermitage—same as before—the white clouds still linger upon the crags.
The maple leaves in the forest have just begun to fall;
the autumn light invites a leisurely stroll.
One knows not whether one's body is far or near.
At evening, I sought lodging in a sacred cavern;
lying down and awakening, the mechanisms of worldly dust were extinguished.
Having forgotten the mind of fame and profit, I remained there.
Even the dreams of the marketplace and the court have ended.
If even this brief visit is like this,
how much more so for one who remains in seclusion for a lifetime?
How to cure nighttime hunger:
one spoonful of mica powder.
Staying overnight at Xilin Temple. Staying overnight at Xilin Temple, as before: the trees have fallen, the sky is clear, and the mountain’s emerald hues unfold.
Loving the mountains, I rode my horse into the hills;
in my heart, I knew I could not equal the Magistrate of Chaisang.
Having stayed one night at Xilin, I sent him back.
Staying overnight at Xilin Temple, I set out early for the assembly of Master Man of Donglin, and thus send this in response to Cui, the Second-and-Twentieth Yuanwai.
Staying overnight at Xilin Temple, I set out early for the assembly of Master Man of Donglin.
Sent by proxy to Vice Director Cui No. 22, with the same sentiments as before: Exiled from the imperial court, we are separated from the *yuánluán* birds;
Grown old, I enter Lushan, following the company of deer.
At the fading twilight, desolate and forlorn, I seek lodging at a temple.
At dawn, I purify myself and await the assembly of monks;
after I rise at the Double Grove, I hear the bell.
On this odd-numbered day, you hasten toward the pavilion.
The heights and depths of the Peng bird and the quail are each predetermined;
do not weary your mind and strength with longing thoughts from afar.
Inscribed on the Hot Springs at the Foot of Mount Lu (same as the previous): A single eye of hot spring water flows toward the east.
Soaking in mud and pouring over weeds, warmth is of no avail.
For what reason does the warm water of Mount Li flow into channels of gold and brickwork?
Ascending Mount Xianglu— on Mount Xianglu, as before, leaning against rocks and climbing over creepers to rest this sickly body;
with a green-stripped bamboo staff and a white silk turban,
when the time comes, I shall paint the barrier of Mount Lu.
This is the person atop Mount Xianglu.

When my thatched cottage was first completed upon descending from Mount Xianglu, I happened to inscribe this on the eastern wall. [When my thatched cottage was first completed upon descending from Mount Xianglu.]
An Impromptu Inscription on the East Wall of My New Thatched Cottage of Five Beams and Three Bays:
Stones guard the pillars of cypress, and stones line the walls.
The southern eaves catch the sun, so that even in winter it is warm.
With its northern-facing doors welcoming the breeze, it is cool in the summer months;
the flying spring waters that sprinkle the steps have but recently fallen silent,
and the slanting bamboo brushing the windows has not yet formed a row.
Next spring, we shall renovate the eastern wing of the reed hut;
with its paper screens and rush curtains, it will be fit for Meng Guang.
A playful gift to Official Li Shisan. (Same as above) Holding the reins as we see you off, you are tipsy with wine.
I see Mount Lu from afar and point it out to you;
I imagine that at first you found joy in following the army,
yet had not yet come to cherish those who dwell atop Mount Xianglu.

Accompanied by various mountain guests, we ascended Mount Xianglu together; encountering rain, we returned drenched and disheveled, laughing and joking with one another as I composed this verse to dispel our embarrassment. Accompanied by various mountain guests.
As before, he returned from Mount Xianglu after encountering rain;
his robes were soaked and disarrayed.
Laughing and jesting with one another, he inscribed this "Exoneration from Ridicule": "Carefree, I went up the mountain;
Limping and decrepit, I returned in the rain."
The steps are perilous as we climb the *pi-li-ye* vines;
the stones are slippery as we tread upon the *mei-tai* moss.
Our socks get soiled, and you jest with me.
I laugh at myself for wearing these shoes;
do not despise these feet of mud,
for they have once trodden upon the jade steps of the palace.
Reading the Poetry of Lingche Reading the poetry of Lingche is the same as before: beneath the western corridor within Donglin Monastery, several poems were inscribed upon stone slabs.
Their phrasing is strange and yet instructive in its distinctiveness.
By looking at his name, one knows him to be the Elder Master Laotang.
Three Quatrains Parting from Caotang, same as before: While listening to the mountain birds, he sleeps facing the sun.
The imperial decree on yellow paper fell before my pillow;
moved by the Emperor’s grace, I must rise for a moment.
I have no intention of dwelling at Mount Lu for many years.
Having long slept in coarse cloth as a layman,
I suddenly donned a crimson robe to become a magistrate;
though my body has emerged from the thatched hall, my mind does not leave Mount Lu.
There is no need for a formal letter of summons;
my three-bay thatched cottage opens toward the mountains,
and a single stream of mountain spring water winds its way around the dwelling.
Do not be sorrowful at the mountain colors and the sound of the water;
when your three-year term as an official has ended, you shall return.
*Inscribed upon Parting at the Caotang of Yiai, Also Presented to Prefect Li (10)*.
Presented together to Lord Li, the Tenth Governor: Li Fang resided constantly at White Deer Grotto on Mount Lu; previously, he lived beneath Lufeng Peak.
His study faced the Medicine Terrace.
The newly cleared path through the ivy has been joined once more.
As before, the bamboo window stands open;
I personally dredge the water at the steps and pluck the lotus from the pond with my own hands.
Only after five years do they arrive for a brief moment;
having stayed but one night, they must return again.
Even if they were not to return permanently, [the time would still pass].
It is still better than not coming at all.
At your family’s White Deer Grotto,
I hear that moss has even begun to grow.
A new pond has been excavated before the thatched hall for raising fish and planting lotuses; every day there is a profound sense of seclusion.
The gurgling sounds of the Three Gorges water flow on.
A vast expanse of ten thousand qing of water does not compare to the surface of New Pond,
where a gentle breeze stirs the rippling waves.
The small duckweed floats and drifts;
the first catkins are falling in profusion.
The red carp are but two or three inches long.
Nine or eight branches of white lotuses wind around the water as if forming a path;
the fence has just been set up to protect the embankment, yet it has already been visited by guests from the mountains.
It is called the White Family Pond.
Expecting white clouds, expecting white clouds; the yellow name was made beneath the crags, as in the previous three cases. The vital energy is too robust;
there is much contention within the breast.
At sixty, the body is too old;
the four limbs can no longer support it.
From forty to fifty—
This is precisely the time for retirement from public service.
With advancing years, one recognizes the lot of fate;
the mind grows weary, and worldly endeavors diminish.
Seeing that my enthusiasm for wine still remains and my strength for climbing mountains has not yet declined,
I am fortunate that my age coincides with this season.
For now, I make an appointment with the white clouds.
Chanting "Leaving the Mountains" (Chushan yin)— the same as the preceding morning's verses on wandering immortals—
I sing the "Returning to the Wei" (Laiwei qu) melody at evening.
Lying amidst the clouds, sitting upon white stones,
I have stayed fifteen nights within the mountains;
now I follow the waters emerging from the cave.
Turning away from other circumstances,
I shall visit the rocky bamboo groves again at dawn and dusk;
my heart aspires to the affinity with the jade grasses.
Inscription on the Tomb of Master Yuan The stone ridges of the ancient tomb are sharp and cold;
Evening clouds coalesce into a still, somber scene.
In vain I mourn for the moon over Tiger Creek.

Not seeing the monk from Yanmen, I send this to Vice President Bao at Donglin Monastery. Sent to Vice President Bao at Donglin Monastery, same as before: In the ancient hall, cool shade; the mountain trees are in spring.
Leaning against a rock by the pond, I gaze upon my own body.
Who can come here to sit and burn incense?
Together we shall become twenty people of Mount Luofeng.
Inscription on the Water Hall of Xilin Temple, Respectfully Sent to Lord Wuyang.
Day after day I love the mountains, yet my return is always late. [Inscription on the Water Hall of Xilin Temple, Respectfully Sent to Lord Wuyang—same as above.]
In leisure, I have idly passed my youth;
this remaining life will surely be spent aging within the woods.
My heart makes its vow with the tall pines and the fragments of stone.
At Jianji Hermitage, as at the former sites, among ancient cypresses and junipers on the rocky walls, monkeys climb and cranes nest where branches have withered and broken.
In the fifth month there is ice; in the sixth month it is cold.
At that time, I saw the immortal coming to gather snow.
Presented at Wulao Peak Daming Hermitage to the Recluse. By Yao Xi. Looking toward this mountain from the north of Yun Guan.
We seldom walk hand in hand with you.
At the edge of the forest we wade across the water;
at the mouth of the cave we enter the slanting glow of the setting sun.
Suddenly I perceive the phoenixes and cranes drawing near;
in an instant, they fly off as mist and clouds.
My old friend is a guest of pure harmony.
Silently I grasp the subtle essence of the lute’s heart;
fortunately, the art of cinnabar may be transmitted to me,
and the Blue Dragon shall surely return.
How long has my life’s journey been?
On this day, we part once more.
At Jianji Hermitage—Jianji Hermitage—the Hall of Master Sun Fang is joined to the clouds.
Amidst the purple mists and azure verdancy,
there must naturally be medicinal herbs;
who would dare say that there are no immortals?
Mossy hues swallow the cliffside paths;
the sound of pines yields to the cascading springs.
Yet, I am unable to depart for long-lasting rest.
Could this indeed be a karmic connection from a former life?
Master Liang, an alchemist and immortal, resided in Qingniugou Valley. Yang Heng followed the clouds as he entered Qingniugou Valley.
The Daoist of the Blue Ox invited me to stay overnight;
how touching, amidst the long night and bright moonlight,
there was but a single bamboo stalk by the altar.
I cherish the hermit of Mount Lu; like the previous verse, the wind sounds the bell beyond the clouds.
Cranes nest in thousand-year-old pines.
Longing for him, he remains unseen in the distance.
The moon rises over the layered mountains;
the waterfalls, waterfalls, flow into the river. This is the true southern face of Mount Lu.
The waterfalls have been renowned since ancient times.
Ten thousand li it journeys toward the blue sea;
A thousand fathoms it emerges from the white clouds.
Its cold sound remains, in the end, ever distant.
Which school of the numinous can claim distinction?
After the Tiantai tradition, the subsequent currents flowed evenly, beyond comparison with one another.
Jianji Grotto: Jianji Grotto is the same as before; having just entered the Mysterious Capital, my pent-up distress is resolved.
Accompanied by feathered immortals, we wander everywhere.
A stream crosses the mouth of the cave, cutting off the dust of the mortal world.
The peaks rise toward the heart of Heaven, where purple qi ascends;
at the golden well, the autumn light of the spring glistens and sparkles;
upon the stone altar, the ancient pines resonate with a desolate and elegant melody.
After finishing my chanting, I sigh once more at the affairs of this fleeting life. [The painting is...
Before Jianji Pavilion—just as before—the courtyard is filled with ashes as the people conclude their incantations.
On the western peak, the cool shadows deepen as the moon sinks low;
arriving here, one speaks of past events from within the stele.
One wanders back and forth by the altar, for autumn is now at its deepest.
Depart for Donglin, depart for Donglin! Upon the peaks of Mount Cao, smoke rises unceasingly;
by the pond, white lotuses remain as companions.
One clearly perceives that the net of worldly dust is but a binding shackle.

One must ride a horse to part from the clouds and springs. Inscribed on the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the third year of Huichang. [This was written by] Cui Dan, who passed the jinshi examination under Emperor Wenzong in the fourth year of Kaicheng; he later served as Secretariat Drafter (Zhongshu Sheren), Vice Minister of Justice and the Ministry of Revenue, and Regional Commander of the Zhongwu Army.
Inscription on a Poem: When I, as the Right Vice-Director, was dispatched to govern Zhongling, my elder brother,
the Director of the Imperial Library, could not bear the long separation and sent a letter to the Chancellor, requesting a replacement for me.
Thus, they were able to travel together to Jiangxi at that time.
The Great Virtue Master Xian of Jianfu, a preeminent leader of the Chan school, said:
"We shall return to Donglin."
I have also had the fortune to form a fellowship with you on the road and accompany you in your travels,
where I have frequently enjoyed your refined discourse.
Now, as I pass by this temple...
I have left behind this one poem as an inscription:
Pai Hui, a courtier of the Lintai Academy, departs from the Secretariat;
The Chan lineage emerges from the imperial capital at the Phoenix Gate.
Returning to the Twin Trees, he personally sought out Huiyuan;
passing by the Five Willows, he paid his respects to Yuanming.
As a layman in white robes, he held the ranks of nobility in light esteem.
Defeated by the high monk’s [pure] emotions, this sick man was led to abandon all external thoughts and serve him as his teacher.

[This is] in response to my younger brother’s inscription for Donglin Temple. In response to my younger brother’s inscription for Donglin Temple: Pei Mo was originally no guest who could "climb the dragon" or "attach to the phoenix."
Originally the body of a mountain ape or wild deer,
you have vainly donned the ancestral sashes within the official ranks;
how could this compare to [living as] the dust of the [wild] fields?
Delighting in being a worthy companion to my jade-like younger brother,
and rejoicing in serving as the cause for [his] golden [attainments],
today I pass beneath the Peak of the Incense Burner.
Just as I rejoice that there are recluses beyond the mundane world,
the Jianji Hermitage— Jianji Guan— by Shen Bin: a mountain treasury of sublime scenery,
where towers and pavilions open upon grotto palaces.
With white hair filling my head, who would be willing to come?
With blue-green moss covering every step, I have come of my own accord.
For three days, the wind-blown sails have cast aside all worldly affairs.
A cup of jade-essence for the thought of eternal life;
on this path, the heart is as bright as the stars and moon.
O immortals of the Apricot Terrace, do not harbor mutual suspicion.
Returning once more to Donglin Monastery—just as before fifteen years ago I came here again.
The pond is deep with moss, the trees hang with vines;
revisiting these various places, my heart is wounded by the passing days.
I do not see the old monk with white hair;
the flowers hold dew beneath the long night moon.
In the hall, there is no wind to stir the lamps that shine through the dawn.
It is truly startling that as one goes, one grows ever older;
there is no certainty whether there will be another coming or not.
The waterfalls flow as before, cascading from the source within the mountain peaks to transform into water.
Spraying forth like a waterfall, a marvel rare in the world;
though it seems as if a celestial maiden has stolen the loom to weave it,
one does not see the mountain man returning with his harvest.
For ten thousand ages, its color has been loathed as thinner than the bright moon;
for a thousand fathoms, it dares to learn the soaring flight of white clouds.
If one says it is truly fit to be cut and fashioned, [it would surely become a robe of honor].
Already purchased by a wealthy family to be made into robes.
Gazing at Mount Lu, gazing at Mount Lu—just as before, he passed through Kuanglu and slept off his wine.
His two eyes hung upon the perilous peaks all day long.
It presses down upon Wu and Chu, encompassing the waters;
it pierces through the clouds and mists, leaning alone against the heavens.
Its precipitous face rises so steeply that there is no path for birds.
Countless peaks wildly desire to pursue the fishing boats;
let the riverfolk not laugh at my lingering gaze.
I have long contemplated seclusion before a waterfall.
Inscription on Donglin Monastery By the layman Zhou Que The Great Zhong Emperor’s grace is profound;
He sent me once more to lead deluded followers to recognize the Buddha-mind.
The half-dead white lotus has just descended from the clouds.
Wishing to restore the desolate ruins, he spread gold upon them;
the monk opened the stone chamber and the sutras were still there.
The tiger’s paw prints on the spring-fed stream have not yet faded from view.
Who would have thought that this traveler with books and sword from the Five Lakes would,
in this life, once again behold Donglin?
Once more he upholds the profound Dharma, like a reflection of the Western Heaven.
The lofty gates open before the ever-new azure peaks;
the wind carries a drifting cloud to beckon the White Horse,
while cranes welcome the poor woman as she offers her gold coins.
The śramaṇa seeking the Buddha has long been familiar with the path;
for those suffering in the ocean of misery, it is easy to find a boat.
The three teachings together flourish, discussing the Way of the Emperor.
The Dazhong era is an era of great peace.

Inscribed at Donglin Monastery. Four poems inscribed at Donglin Monastery by the Great Master Guanhui of Chan Yue: Wandering idly, sitting idly, I contemplate the攀缘 (pān-yuan, *ālambana*—objects of attachment).
Mostly situated before the ancient temple of Donglin,
the small waterfalls rise to a height of three hundred feet;
the short pines are mostly one thousand years old.
Lu Lengjia’s paintings of mossy crags are now but sketches;
Yin Zhongkan’s stele has been pierced by raindrops.
Now I wish to once again honor the Lotus Society and depart.
I know not who these ancient worthies may be;
white sandalwood flowers drip with dew,
and the green *bhiṣmaka* grass is shrouded in fragrance.
In this field of earth, not even a speck of dust remains.
What kind of person is worthy to dwell within it?
A jade image in a pearl shrine, with incense clouds drifting across.
Brocade-like clouds often grow beside the stone altars;
where is the snake-warding practitioner now?
On the mountain peaks, one hears only the cries of doves.
The ancient imperial carriage stretches across the void as lingering clouds dampen it;
at the solitary tomb of Yaśas, the setting sun lingers long.
There stands an old monk leaning against a pine tree.
Fearing that someone might steal the white monkey child;
the various practitioners of Xilin Mountain share this sentiment. Who else besides those on the island before is so intimate?
The various peaks are its very neighbors.
White-haired, he rests his cold head upon the stone;
his azure sleeves are untainted by the waves.
Acorns and chestnuts are piled along the walking path.
The monkey circles the body in meditative concentration;
suddenly, he again forms a society.
May he become the one who sweeps the altar.
Inscription on Donglin Monastery By the Monk Qi Ji of Jingmen Before the peaks and beneath the groves lie the monasteries of the east and west;
From the ends of the earth and the farthest reaches come monks who pass to and fro.
In this world of leisure, springs and rocks flow in stillness.
Clouds and pines are cold and damp; incense and lamps burn through the day.
How can these compare to the Great Being’s restoration of the community?
It is fitting that all worthy ones should further apply themselves with devotion.
Once I stayed in a neighboring room, hanging my staff and water jar;
there, the clamor of mountain rivulets was heard as they melted the spring ice.
The Hall of Master Huiyuan—The Hall of Master Huiyuan is the same as the former one by the side of the White Lotus Pond.
Liu Lei’s wind and bone are entirely dragon-like;
together they slight the nobility of the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords,
and alike they cherish our Master as the one who is long in the Way of the Dharma.
The Prefect of Tao was often too drunk to be summoned;
Lord Xie’s mind was so distracted that he had no way to enter.
Who today can reach this point and contemplate their lofty footsteps?
The wind is silent as moss overruns the plastered walls;
at Jianji Hermitage— Jianji Hermitage, as described before— one sees the reflections of clouds and mists across ten thousand valleys and hears the sound of pines and cypresses for a thousand years.
How can one teach those of inferior capacity to easily believe in rebirth?
It is as white as the moon together with the void.
The incense blends with the clear air;
idly seeking the paintings on the ancient corridors,
I recall the names of the ranked immortals.
Luo Xing Temple The same as before: For what reason did this star descend from the azure heavens?
It alone transformed into a monastic dwelling, vast and remote.
As the rain retreats from the pavilions and towers, the green ridges grow cold.
The wind from the open window carries the fragrance of white artemisia;
Autumn passed, wild geese fly across the vast desert.
The moon shines coldly as the waves roar through the night hall.
Leaning on the railing all day long, I idly cast my gaze afar;
suddenly, I suspect my body has been transported to the Xiao and Xiang rivers.
To the west of the monastery is the Water Pavilion; to the west of the monastery is the Water Pavilion (as before). The pine and cypress trees connect with the ancient pagoda.
The window railing is left open at will;
water winds through the midst of cool shade.
People come from the heat.
Chirping crickets accompany the wind as cicadas bear the herons;
leaning trees and rocks are covered with moss.
Toward dawn, beneath the Eastern Grove.
Reluctantly departing from this place, I inscribe these couplets at Donglin Monastery. Couplets Inscribed at Donglin Monastery: The ancient hall stands majestic, commanding the azure peaks;
The spiritual responses of the Jin dynasty reveal its divine traces.
Wild birds in the forest startle at the dawn *brahmā*-chant;

a solitary monkey on the ridge listens to the evening bell. At this time, the Military Commissioner, Acting Grand Marshal, and Chief Councilor Xu Zhizheng, observes that geese are cold as mist rises over the morning railing.
Autumn moon over Tiger Creek illuminates the cold pines; a monk in purple robes respectfully burns incense as it drifts into the jeweled hall, enshrouding the golden image.
A cypress leans against the pine-window, sheltering the jade-like countenance. The Daoist Li Xuan gazes at the vibrant flowers clinging to the half-rock, as if in love with them.
Deer sleep amidst the lush grass of the deep valley; the Censor-in-Chief, Grand Master of the Purple Gold Fish Sash, Li You, observes that where monks halt their staffs, all minds are Buddha.
Old trees support the mist with a form like dragons; the Censor-in-Chief, Grand Master of the Scarlet Fish Sash, Wang San, notes that bamboo shades the Zen gate as the azure mists merge.

Mist swirls through the secluded paths, where moss seals the ground; the Judicial Secretary and Military Aide manage the petitions and memorials. Clear streams wind around the steps, their pure sounds echoing afar;
tiered ridges lead toward the gate, ever more bustling with travelers.
How much more so for one who loves the dustless realm, chanting as he visits these empty passes without weariness!

Once, while idly strolling with my attendants and the monks and Daoists of the monastic compound, we composed verses together.
On the subject of Donglin, there are two poems. By Great Master Kuangbai of Wéntong: "How long-lasting are the fine vistas of Donglin!"
The orchids grow in many places and are fragrant;
it is a pity that worldly people cannot come to them.
What harm is there in letting them age among the clouds and trees?
The azure heavens lean against the sky as the clear light faces the door;
the murmuring waters fall into the mouth of the stream, circling the corridor at night.
Upon reaching this place, one can do nothing but resolve to re-establish the religious society.
Do not dwell on other trivial matters.
At Donglin, following the four previous verses,
the scenery is even more serene and secluded.
The guests of the shrine depart and do not return;
the clouds over Zhongfeng peak are autumnal.
The pines wither and the troops of monkeys disperse.
The mountain stream flows over large logs and fallen trees;
I await the time to plan my retirement,
so that I may come once more to lie upon this stone pavilion.
People resemble cranes and red deer;
matters on the road are as tangled as hemp.
The stones grow heavy with lingering rain.
In this Cangqing Water Rhapsody, the long pines shed their emerald hues.
Do not say that in this place there is no portion for me,
a man of the fallen dynasty.
I lived for a long time in the home of Huichi.
I traveled extensively through Mount Luoxing and its surrounding areas;
then I came south to the regions of Wu and Chu.
Accidentally ascending a temple within the lake,
I suspect I have reached a mountain in the midst of the sea.
A solitary tree is lush with damp, clinging vines.
White birds rest idly on the distant marshes;
at last, I bid farewell to this floating world.
Reclining high upon my bed, I listen to the murmuring stream.

The Stele for the Late Venerable Vinaya Master Bi of Xiqia Monastery, Tang Dynasty; Inscribed on the Thirteenth Day of the Fifth Month in the Jiachen Year of the Changqing Era. Compiled by Liu Ke, Court Consultant, Censor of the Imperial Chancery (acting as a Censor), and Grand Marshal of the Upper Pillar State; calligraphed by the Śramaṇa Yungao; the title inscribed in seal script by Qi Yu, Acting Magistrate of Huaining County in Shuzhou, formerly serving as Sub-Prefectural Administrative Officer of the Hongzhou Prefectural Government. [The Inscription] The Buddha-Dharma is profound and subtle, its essence vast and boundless. It is that which the Tathāgatas have transmitted, the path upon which the Bodhisattvas tread. Since the beginning of time, it has been the source of the myriad phenomena; throughout the three periods, it has been the foundation of all things. Its manifestations are inexhaustible, yet its ultimate principle is singular. To speak of its form is to fall into the trap of words; to describe its substance is to stray from the realm of the mind. In the land of the Great Tang, there was a man named Bi, whose secular surname was Li. He was born in the region of Jiangdong and grew up amidst the refinements of the capital. From his youth, he possessed a spirit of detachment; in his maturity, he cultivated a heart of compassion. He sought the Way through the scriptures and realized the truth through meditation. His conduct was pure and his discipline was strict. He maintained the precepts with unwavering resolve and taught the Dharma with tireless diligence. He served as the Vinaya Master at Xiqia Monastery in the capital. There, he guided the assembly, harmonized the community, and ensured that the monastic rules were observed without flaw. His reputation spread far and wide, reaching the imperial court. He was summoned to the palace to lecture on the scriptures, where his eloquence was praised by the Emperor and his virtue was esteemed by the nobility. Later, he retired to the mountains to seek solitude. He dwelt in seclusion at Xiqia Monastery, where he lived a life of simplicity and austerity. He spent his days in silent contemplation and his nights in the recitation of sutras. He remained steadfast until the end of his life, never wavering in his commitment to the Triple Gem. On the thirteenth day of the fifth month of the Jiachen year of the Changqing era, he passed away peacefully at the age of [number]. His disciples mourned his departure, and the local authorities lamented the loss of a great teacher. To commemorate his virtues and ensure that his legacy would endure, this stele was erected. The world is filled with those who seek fame and profit, yet few are those who truly understand the Way. Master Bi was one of the rare few who possessed both wisdom and integrity. His teachings remain a beacon for future generations. May his merit extend to all beings, leading them toward liberation. [End of Inscription] *Note: The original text contains a lacuna regarding the Master’s age at death.*

Record of Mount Lu, Volume Five. Proofread once. Do not alter the characters. Based on the Gao-shan Temple manuscript of the five-volume *Record of Mount Lu*.
Volumes two and three are Song-dynasty woodblock editions.
The remaining three fascicles were supplemented by an old transcription;
however, all characters bearing the taboo names of the Song dynasty have been omitted from them.
This is likely because they also derived from Song editions.
In this book, characters avoided as taboo names were omitted up to the character "ch'an" (栴), which was the taboo name of Emperor Gaozong;
however, the character "dun" (敦), a homophone of the taboo name of Emperor Guangzong, was not missing its strokes.
This indicates that it was carved during the reigns of Emperors Gaozong and Guangzong.
This work was published in the Shoushan Ge Congshu series as a copy from the Siku Quanshu; however, only the first three chapters remain as a single fascicle.
The compilers of the Imperial Library noted that the fourth and fifth chapters were lost.
Now, the Song-era woodblock edition actually consists of eight chapters and five fascicles.
Chapters one and two constitute Fascicle One;
Chapter Three constitutes Fascicle Two.
The fourth and fifth chapters constitute Volume Three;
the sixth chapter constitutes Volume Four;
and the seventh and eighth chapters constitute Volume Five.
The Shushankaku edition not only lacks the fourth chapter and those following,
but its division of fascicles also differs from the original version of that period.
According to the palace officials, the current text consists of a single fascicle.
To then suspect that only four or five scrolls were lost is,
moreover, an error.
It is unknown when this entire work was lost by more than half.
The palace officials remarked that even the *Yongle Dadian* manuscript contained only three chapters;
thus, the edition published in the Eastern Country had already been lost since the early Ming dynasty.
In addition to the Song woodblock edition,
there is also a complete copy of the 1707 (Genroku 10) printed edition.
Now, I have selected both the Genroku and Shuzan editions.
Upon collating [the manuscript] with the Song edition,
I found that although the Genroku edition was complete, it also contained errors and omissions;
the Shuzankaku edition, however, was even more severely corrupted and incomplete.

The first section, "Shushanbon," appropriates Huiyuan’s *Record of Mount Lu* (Lushan ji), omitting portions and briefly citing its variations for several dozen lines; the second section, "Eituzhu" and below, is not appropriated from the Genroku edition.

In the Genroku edition, more than ten lines are misplaced; however, the Shuzan edition is not in error. Furthermore, the Record of Master Yuan states that the passage from "Up to [the character] Yi" describes the scenic excellence of Shimen for more than ten lines.
Furthermore, the aforementioned record by Master Yuǎn states that "the three types of conduct" refers to those such as the Arhats;
both the Shǒushān manuscript and the Zhùyì manuscript omit this.
In the third section, thirteen characters—beginning with "Formerly, Sēngmiǎo of Dōnghǎi said..."—are omitted from the Shǒushān manuscript.
Furthermore, twenty-eight characters beginning with "Again, regarding the source of the merit...
from the sixth fascicle of the Genroku edition are missing;
and in the seventh fascicle of the Genroku edition, there is a description of errors found in various steles at Tōrin-ji Temple.

The inscriptions for the Sūtra Repository of Donglin Temple and the Stele Inscription for the Great Virtuous Master Can are placed before the three steles of Dharma Master Huiyuan and others; from this,
one can see that the Genroku edition already cannot be considered free of errors.
This original manuscript lacks the second leaf of fascicle one; fascicle four lacks both the twenty-first and twenty-eighth leaves.
Furthermore, in fascicle one, Li Chang’s preface was written on the third leaf along the binding edge.
Thus, two leaves at the beginning of this [text] should also have been lost;
now, the second leaf of the first scroll has been supplemented according to the Genroku edition.
As for the other leaves, even the Genroku edition is missing them.
In this world of resentment, there is ultimately no other basis upon which to rely for supplementation.
I have long cherished this book;
its narrative is elegant and comprehensive.
